utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom, General Galic, Defence counsel, Prosecution, and also those who are assisting us present as always because we are fully aware that we couldn't do anything without your assistance interpreting or giving the technical support we need. We are here today for the Pre-Defence Conference in accordance with the Rule 73 ter, and it is important to see where we stand at this very moment in respect of several issues on which we received motions from -- or submissions from both parties. I would like to start with the easy ones, I would say. Disclosure matters, could the parties inform the Chamber what happened since the last Status Conference on the 20th of September where there was some problems still with the disclosure of newspaper articles, books and parts of them on their way to be translated, as far as I remember. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. The parties met yesterday afternoon and discussed those various matters. As well, the Prosecution received a letter from the Defence dated the 24th of September 2002. If I could go through some of the issues which we raised at the last mention and progress on them. We indicated on the last occasion that there were some 130 entries on the Defence exhibit list for which we did not have copies, in other words, disclosure had not been made. The Defence, in its letter of the 24th of September, re-affirmed that they had indeed provided those documents to us. We maintain we have not received them, having checked the entries alongside our record of what we received from the Defence. Mr. President, the problem I think is partly explained by the fact that the confirming letter, signed by the Prosecution, as to what it has received and which is drafted by the disclosing party does not set out any detail as to the documents which have been handed over with the exception of a disclosure made on the 26th of April, 2001. So we have asked the Defence to simply provide us with copies of those documents. Secondly, on the 19th of September, the Defence provided to the Prosecution three cardboard folders of documents which comprised what appeared to be original B/C/S documents together with translations. Having checked those, a number of those documents do not appear on the exhibit list and indeed the Defence confirmed yesterday that it was their intention and their belief that those documents were on the exhibit list. So that is the second problem with disclosure of the exhibit list. The Defence has informed us that they will make some enquiries. We will let them know which of those documents are not on the exhibit list to save some time. But the Prosecution remains concerned that disclosure has not yet been made of items on the exhibit list. Moving on to the topic of videos and books. On the last occasion, Mr. President, that is on the 20th of September, you indicated that within ten days the Prosecution should be informed of the parts of the six books and the videotapes which the Defence intended to tender. That has not happened. Indeed, we still have received only four books, not six. I raised that with the Defence yesterday and I understand that, in due course, that they will inform us but we will appreciate knowing as soon as possible. The letter of the 24th of September in relation to videotapes informed us that the parts on which the Defence relies have been sent for translation and in due course we will receive the translations of the relevant parts of the videotapes. The letter also informed us that in relation to the translation of exhibit entries generally, that at this stage, the Defence does not require our assistance in obtaining rough translations. Mr. President, as to the newspaper articles, we have confirmed that we have received the 16 newspaper articles. We are not sure that we had received translations, but we are checking that. So I don't raise that as an issue at this point until we have completed our checks as to the translation of the newspaper articles. In relation to the letter which was sent out by the Defence dated the 30th of September informing us of the first six witnesses and anticipated exhibits, the list of exhibits indicates there are none, however, two videotapes will be presented, but not tendered into evidence, and I read those words from the chart which accompanies the letter. The Prosecution inquired of the Defence the identity of those tapes, in other words, which of the disclosed tapes are they, because there is no identification which has been provided to us. We are informed that in relation to the videotape that pertains to the second witness in the order of witnesses to be called, that the Defence received that last weekend, indeed has not disclosed it to us. In relation to the second videotape, I am told by the Defence that they will confirm precisely which of the disclosed videotapes it relates to, and by reference to what appears on the videotape, which of three parts, three possible parts it will be. The difficulty we have with that, I understand it relates to an interview of the witness, is of course we don't have a translation, we don't know what the witness looks like, and it is rather unsatisfactory as a method, a methodology of informing us with precision as to what is to be tendered. Mr. President, you also on the last occasion indicated that you wanted the parties to reconsider the issue of agreed facts. There was a filing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would rather deal with that as a separate issue and first concentrate on disclosure matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any observations from the Defence in respect to what has been said by the Prosecution? Is it a good reflection of what has been discussed yesterday and is there any comment to be made on the, may I say, the complaints about the first part of the trial to start? Perhaps we first start with the disclosure issues in general, so not concentrated on the next week, such as the concern of the Prosecution that now documents are disclosed which were not yet on the list, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes Mr. President. Good morning to everyone. We took note of this observation. Yesterday I asked from the Prosecution to give us an example so that we know what happened, and the Prosecution was not able to do it. So I found out, with great relief, this morning that the Prosecution would give us a list of these pieces of the documents so that we can see whether perhaps this is a misunderstanding between us, which is always possible, or too that it is just an error on our part, just a material error which is also possible, and, therefore, we will make progress in this direction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When will the parties further discuss this matter? Because I hear that the Defence is not yet convinced that documents were disclosed which were not on their list, as far as I understand; while I hear from the Prosecution that such documents were disclosed not appearing on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is no point in the parties meeting to discuss the 130 documents of which we advised the Defence two weeks ago. There is nothing more the parties do about that. The Defence simply maintains they have been disclosed; we maintain they have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could they be redisclosed. If the documents are there, 130 documents, it would take me one hour behind a copying machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As to the second bundle, that is the documents disclosed on the 19th of September which the Defence thought were on the exhibit list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- We have done a check of those, and we could meet after the conference this morning and give them, if they wish, some examples so they can satisfy themselves that they have a problem. It is a matter for the Defence to amend its exhibit list and by simply checking whether they have indeed included those documents on the exhibit list. We are happy to assist however we can, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I expect the parties to do is to check whether the, at least the examples indicated by the Prosecution, whether they appear on the exhibit list. If they do not, and if the Prosecution is able to demonstrate that they are not on the list, the Chamber expects a revised list. Then, the 130 documents not yet been disclosed, I think the Chamber is not that much interested to hear about who, for what reasons claims that they were disclosed and who contests that they were disclosed. 130 documents, could you give me an approximate number of pages? Are these all one-page documents? I mean, are we talking about 13.000 pages or 260 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: More like 260 pages, Mr. President, and we understand mostly one or two-page documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that 260 pages could be copied in approximately one hour while further discussions on whether disclosed or not might easily take two hours. So it will save you one hour for the parties to -- and if not, I will call a meeting with the parties, ask them to give me the 260 documents, ask them to wait for one hour, and I will -- the Chamber will copy them so that the problem is solved. We are here to solve the problems, rather to exploit them any further. Any other comments specifically in relation to the specificity -- the no exhibits appearing on the list for next week while it has been indicated that videotapes will be played although not tendered. But it is not clear to the Prosecution what they can expect. Is there any comment in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the proposal of the Defence to show video material through one witness, and we do not intend to tender this material, it is the second witness on the list. I told to my colleagues that I have received this material when I recently travelled to Banja Luka and I will do my best to turn it over to my colleagues on the other side on Monday. I also said that it is a very brief video material. There is no text, simply an illustration. In our list, we also stated that we may use that video material in case it is ready, and as far as the video material proposed to be shown through the last witness on the list, that video material has been disclosed to the Prosecution. We also have an audio transcript of that material, and I told the Prosecution that I will turn over to them tomorrow the tape, together with the transcript. In view of the fact that tomorrow is Friday we believe that one-week deadline was complied with because that witness is the last witness on our list. And again, regarding that witness who is the last witness on our list there is a dilemma whether he will be able to come here on Tuesday, because he has some health problems but at any rate, we will disclose that videotape on -- on Tuesday, we will disclose that tape, on Tuesday. So I believe that my colleagues will be able to prepare adequately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Piletta-Zanin disappearing just for private reasons or is there any specific --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for a second. Just for a second. He offers his apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that you recently received a videotape with no text, and you would use only a small portion of it, and you would disclose it to the Prosecution next Monday. Could that not be done a bit quicker? I mean, it is just copying a small portion of a videotape, just pictures, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have the tape on Saturday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you only receive it on Saturday morning. Okay. I cannot force you to copy a tape which is not in your possession. This, of course, indicating material arrived late does not automatically entail that finally it will be, the material will be accepted, if it would be tendered, or even if it would just be played, if the Prosecution has had no opportunity to look at it. So accepting it at this very moment, not the Chamber, of course, is not in a position to say that you have to copy a videotape which you have not in your hands yet, but this cannot be understood as a decision on whether you could use it. That is an entirely different matter. So we will look at the material, and we will hear the objections. If the disclosure, in the view of the Prosecution, has been too late, and we will then consider that matter. The Chamber is a bit concerned about the late submission of material.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, I have just arrived last night, and the tape I received on Saturday of Banja Luka is one and a half hour long, however, I left the tape there so some technical issues can be solved because I just need one small detail from the whole tape, and this is why I will not receive the tape before Saturday. So there was a technical reason behind this and behind the fact that we took this course. I expect that I will be able to turn the tape over on Saturday to the other side. I also wish to say that in case there is a problem, I will inform my colleagues that we were unable to prepare this video material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything else to be said about the present stage of the disclosure? The Chamber heard the concerns. We cannot solve all the problems right away, but one of the problems, I mean the 260 pages is certainly an issue which can be solved and not spent time on it again arguing on whether one party could blame the other, or the other the one for being not specific enough on its lists, or not having copied it in time. The Chamber wants this problem to be solved. If not, I will do it myself. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say that during the disclosure proceedings when Defence was disclosing material, we never once received any single complaint from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution, complaining that there was a discrepancy between the list and the materials provided. And I am very surprised that now, at the very end of this disclosing procedure, and just before the beginning of the Defence case, this has been brought up. I will try to inform my colleagues today as to whether we do have these documents and whether we are able to have them copied. But as I said, we have never received any complaints from them before. We are talking about 260 pages, not about a page or two. So this is why we are surprised that this has been brought up just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is my understanding, but if I am wrong, Mr. Ierace, please tell me, is that one of the reasons there was no complaints is that the list was not specific enough so that the Prosecution could not identify at the very moment that documents were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: With the exception of disclosure of April 2001, there were no lists. There were simply a few sentences inviting the Prosecution to agree that they had received bundles of documents relating to certain topics. Therefore, we are only aware of the issues when we have before us the exhibit list and we check that we do not have copies of those documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the understanding of what the reasons were for the Prosecution that they could not identify this problem at an earlier stage seems to be correct. This problem should be solved. Now, we move to another issue. Is there any progress made in respect of the authenticity of potential exhibits? Has the Prosecution checked whether the Defence could expect any complaints about authenticity or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I raise that issue at the meeting yesterday, and in summary, I pointed out that it was of no use to the Prosecution to go to the repository in Banja Luka since it is apparent from those letters from those authorities that much of their documents they have received from the Defence. So seeing the same documents there and indeed which they have copied to us, to both sides, does nothing to establish the authenticity of the documents. I have also pointed out that it seems from the 65 ter summary of the proposed Defence witnesses, that they are not calling any evidence to establish the authenticity of the documents they seek to tender. Finally, I pointed out that unless we have information from them as to where these documents were located with precision, not just across Republika Srpska, but rather places and individuals and we have an opportunity to speak to them in order to establish how they came into their possession and so on, we cannot concede the authenticity of these documents. I should make clear that when I refer broadly to "documents" I am referring to documents which purport on their face to be official documents issued within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I don't make any complaint in relation to newspaper articles. As far as the videos go, video tends to speak for itself to a certain point. Once we have more information about the videos, such as translations and so on, I will be able to say something more sensible about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask comment from the Defence? It is my recollection that Defence repeatedly stressed that testimony about the source of the documents would not be enough, but even the originals would have to be presented. There are several rulings of the Chamber that that was not necessary. But could the Defence inform the Chamber about how they would deal with specifically the source of the documents as far as we understand retrieved by the Defence itself, and then handed over to the -- to some archives in Banja Luka? Is it true that there are no -- there will be no evidence presented on the source of these documents? Could you inform the Chamber about how the Defence intends to deal with that authenticity issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during this trial, I noted on several occasions that the documents found by the Defence investigators in different locations, and I also informed the Trial Chamber that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had been disbanded and in the areas where there were military facilities, the barracks in Nevesinje and so on, our investigators found in these locations documents pertaining to Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And the original of these documents were submitted to the archives of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. So we disclosed the copies of these documents to the Prosecution. And yesterday was the first time when my learned colleague brought up the authenticity of these documents and how we were going to prove it. All I can say is that some of these documents have already been admitted into evidence through Prosecution witnesses. And at that point, my learned friends had no objections to the authenticity. These -- the documents that are, in fact, reports of the corps from December 1992. I don't want to go now into explaining through which witnesses these documents were tendered and then later admitted, but if this presents a problem then the Defence is prepared to have our investigators confirm the authenticity of these documents before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps it will save some time if I can simply illustrate the problem. In the Prosecution case, the Defence, from time to time, complained about the reliability of some medical reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The Prosecution called evidence in relation to the reliability and authenticity of those medical reports, but more to the point, the Prosecution made it clear where those -- through the evidence, where the documents could be located in Sarajevo. It was always open to the Defence if they wished to go to the hospitals, to go to the storing, the storage authorities in Sarajevo to locate and view whatever other records there were. In the same sense, in the same way, what the Prosecution specifically seeks are the details of those individuals, the barracks, the officers, who provided these documents, who handed them over, some informations to when they were handed over so that the Prosecution investigators can go to these people, speak to them, and make their own inquiries in order to work out if these documents can indeed be relied upon. How were they stored over the last six or seven or eight years and so on. That is what we seek. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there are two issues, as a matter of fact. The first issue is whether the copies presented to the Prosecution are copies of the documents at this moment in the archives or stored wherever. That is the same issue as we had in respect of the medical records that have been presented by the Prosecution. That is, if one of the parties would check and compare these documents with the copies they received, that they know where to find them. The second issue is a totally different issue, and that is, who created them, who kept them for quite some time, when they were received, by whom they were received, given by what authority or what individual to the investigator. Wouldn't it be appropriate that since the presence at this moment of these documents in Banja Luka seems not to be the major problem, but that the Prosecution is, as far as authenticity is concerned, mainly focussing on where they came from, when they were produced, received by whom. And since the Defence indicates that they have been retrieved by their investigators, that, for example, a 92 bis statement perhaps would be a good start to get information on the authenticity in this respect. And then, of course, the next step might be that even the investigator in the 92 bis statement says that he received them at the 30th of July in 1998 from Mr. X or Mr. Y. That is always an opportunity that if there is serious doubt as to the authenticity, that then perhaps the source of these documents could be, either by testimony or by written statements, could give further information as to the creation of these documents, et cetera. So it is suggested, in order to prevent any long authenticity debates, that the Defence prepares, perhaps by 92 bis statements, and perhaps also the Prosecution could communicate with the Defence what exactly they would like to know in order to be satisfied that the documents are authentic. I mean it's of no use to seek a 92 bis statement just containing 80 per cent of the information the other party thinks would be necessary. So the concerns about authenticity or source of the documents could be communicated to the parties so we will not lose any time on incomplete information at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I fear that this may become an issue where there is much swapping of information, but not to an extent that allows the Prosecution to make its inquiries. If the Defence was prepared to make their investigators available to the Prosecution investigators so they could sit down and talk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- We would be happy to do it in that informal way. The ultimate concern is simply we need enough information to find out where they came from so we can go there and speak to whoever handed them over. And that might be the fastest and simplest way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is even most, perhaps the most efficient way. Would the Defence be prepared to let their investigators give, in an informal way, the information the investigators of the Prosecution -- Prosecutor would need in order to verify the sources of these documentary material?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to get in touch with my investigators as soon as possible. I just wish to underscore they only have one investigator, because the second investigator who was also on the case, he has just been engaged as the main Defence counsel before this Tribunal in another case. So this will leave me with one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think if he was your investigator at that time, he could provide the investigators of the Prosecution with the information. But I do understand you say I have to be in touch with the investigators, but of course the investigators are assisting the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Assisting of the counsel. So I take it the Defence counsel will such give a positive response as a matter of principle to the suggestion of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was the issue of the authenticity of potential exhibits. The Chamber would very much like to be informed about the progress made in this respect. Next issue, points of agreement. At the Status Conference, we, unfortunately, had to establish that in the attempts made already quite some time ago before the Prosecutions case started finally never succeeded in a longer list of -- and only a very short list. Has any progress been made whether it be on confrontation lines or whatever or the beginning of the conflict or -- so that we could save time and not hear any evidence on facts that are, between the parties, not contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I raised this issue yesterday and the Defence indicated that they preferred to wait until the decision on the application under Rule 98 bis was handed down. With that in mind, we agreed to meet tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Early afternoon, to discuss the matter further. As to the appropriate process, I propose that since the Prosecution had now presented its case, the Defence could perhaps indicate what in the Prosecution case they didn't dispute and we could do it that way. It would be difficult for the Prosecution to make specific proposals as to what might not be contentious. The issue also of, perhaps, the involvement of an officer of the Trial Chamber or a Judge was also discussed in a preliminary fashion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps sometimes the presence of a third person would -- could promote progress to be made by the parties. This, perhaps, is also the point where I should express the regret of the Chamber that where we intended to have the decision on the 98 bis motion to be filed yesterday, that unfortunately we were not able to do it. We expect it to be filed today, so that the parties could continue their efforts with a better understanding of what the present position is. Then the next issue would be the translation of documents. We heard that approximately 50 per cent of the documents were translated, that there were still some concerns. Is there any new information in respect of translation of documents to be tender said?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Only from the Prosecution end that in the letter dated the 24th of September, the Defence have indicated they do not need the assistance of the Prosecution to translate documents to be tendered at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this stage. So I expect that there will be no problems that would prevent us from continuing at this stage. Yes. One of the other issues would be the application of Rule 84. The Chamber is not yet informed about whether we could expect a statement, because no opening statement has been made by the Defence at the beginning of the trial, whether the Chamber could expect a statement being made before the presentation of the Defence evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before Ms. Pilipovic gives you the answer to this question, perhaps this is just in relation to the translations. We see that it is a little late, and that there could be some problems in a sense that some of the annexes that were supporting material for the expert reports, some of them are in Russian, which is the case of one report. Then some of them are in Serbian-Croatian or other languages. And these documents are just annexes. These are supporting documents and they haven't been translated. These are the problems that we could have, and I thought I would just bring it up in case it is important. And in relation to the question in relation to Rule 84, there will be certainly an opening statement by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication on how much time that statement would approximately take?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I spoke to my learned colleagues and also had a question by them, and our answer was that we will -- we will speak -- we will make our opening statement for two and a half hours, maximum. I also informed my colleagues that Defence will be using some maps and some video material that we will hand over to our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. colleagues in due course and also I got in touch with the translation service, and I believe that on Monday if we start in the afternoon, I will be able to provide the interpreters with the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean the written version of the opening statement so that they have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information, Ms. Pilipovic. The annexes, sometimes annexes take five times the volume of a report; sometimes the report takes five times the volume of the annexes. Could you give us some indication on what -- are they smaller annexes or are these huge annexes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a very reasonable amount of pages that I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what is reasonable, what is not reasonable is I think to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that it will be reasonable for the Chamber. We are not talking about a large amount of additional material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These annexes, I am expecting that they will have titles. I think one of the first things that could be done is that the titles, if they are not yet translated and the report itself, that at least the Prosecution knows what these annexes are about, or does that become clear from the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the annexes will be part of the expert reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what I would like to know, that if there are annexes, sometimes it becomes clear from the report what the annexes are about. Sometimes they are just annexes and you have to guess what the relation of the annexes to the report is. Is it clear from the reports what the annexes contain or what is their content, what is their meaning in relation to the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, newspaper articles that my colleague spoke about, and they will be used within the report by one of our experts. These are newspapers that are pointing to the content of the report. So these are newspaper articles that the expert uses to write his report. The only problem is, is that there are about 20 newspaper articles. They have -- they are not in English, that is, they are not in a language that would help my colleague to read the newspaper articles. So this is -- this was underlined in our talks as the problem of translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, that these annexes are newspaper articles is new to the Chamber. We had no idea. I know that most newspaper articles are not 50 or 60 pages, but usually just shorter text. Is there any other issue concerning translation that needs attention at this moment? If not, and having dealt with Rule 84, perhaps we come to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Before we leave the issue of translation, there is a related issue. In relation to the parts of the books that are to be tendered, and, therefore, the translations of those parts, when I inquired yesterday as to progress on that, and that fell within the ten-day time limit that you set on the 20th of September, I was simply informed that there was no progress, and there was no suggestion of any date by which that would be accomplished, and of course, an even more primary issue is that we have only received four of the six books. Could I suggest in relation to the remaining two books if the Defence remains of the view that they have given us six books, perhaps they could indicate within say by Monday, the dates on which they say they gave us the books, and also the titles. I certainly recollect the Defence handing to me personally four books on one occasion and not six. Secondly, I think there needs to be a time limit by which the relevant parts of the six books are communicated to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could you please respond to that observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will, in any case, give these answers to our colleagues in relation to the books by Monday. My reports that I have say that six books have so far been disclosed to the colleagues. I will check this. As far as the translations are concerned from the books that we intend to use, the Defence will do what they -- in accordance with the order of the Chamber, so that every part from the book will be handed over to the colleagues seven days before the witness, unless, of course, my learned colleagues wish to have these parts well before, and I will do my best to hand them over before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let that be clear that the general rule that disclosure should be complete and that only in cases of urgency that disclosure should not be later than seven days before and the indication of what documents will be tendered should not be later than seven days before. But the seven days' rule is not the general rule on disclosure, it is just the exception. Then the Chamber would not like to be confronted again with any discussions on four or six books. It should be clear at this moment that all parts of the six books indicated should be in the hands of the Prosecution. If they are not, let's not spend time on lengthy discussions on whether they should be there or not, but let's, if necessary, copy again the relevant pages so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we leave that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Do I understand it, we don't even have the titles of the six books which makes it very difficult for us to find out what we -- what we should have, and that is apparent from the first provisional list. It simply says, passages from six books regarding relevant events from war in Bosnia. So if not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't imagine that this way of presenting your material could create quite some confusion. Could you give us the titles of the books, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first book, one of the first books, is "The Suffering of Serbs in Sarajevo" and this book is both in Serbian and in English. And this was disclosed by the Defence. The second book, and I think two books are by Mr. Stjepan Siber that we already used, one book is by Mr. Kerim Lucarevic and I think that one book is by Sir Michael Rose, which is also available in English, and I think at the moment, we have five books here. I will check if there are any more books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope that you understand that if there is any discussion about four or six books and that when asked, you come to five, I know that it is the average between four and six. But it is not very precise. It is also not clear to me whether, for example, you would count the book on the suffering of the Serbs in Sarajevo, your B/C/S version is one book and the English translation is another book; or whether that is one book of which two versions exist?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One book. It is one book, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you might even be short of two books at this very moment. But, I mean, you know what books you want to use, whether there are four or six or seven or three or five, let's make sure that the relevant parts of the books that you are going to use are within 36 hours in the hands of the Prosecution. Perhaps first check the Prosecution could tell you what books they have in their entirety then they might tell you whether they know what the passages are, whether they are aware of the passages you would like to use, and then whatever is missing, you try to find the books or at least the passages you want to rely upon so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expect that we will resolve this problem in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's even quicker than 36 hours. Thank you for that. Then, is there any other translation or it was both the translation and the disclosure issue, as a matter of fact, to be discussed at this very moment? May I also ask you, Ms. Pilipovic, in respect of next week, before we come to the list of witnesses, whether the, I would say the logistics of the witnesses are causing any problems as far as next week is concerned? I mean transportation well whatever, problem from home, up until arrival in The Hague and appearance in this court?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, the cooperation between the representatives of the Defence and the VWU is satisfactory, and as far as I have been informed, there have been no problems arising from the witnesses who should arrive in The Hague next week. The only thing is that the last witness who had a visa, received a visa is at a conference so he is not sure whether he will be arriving on Tuesday or Thursday. Also, I was informed that there was a list of the witnesses that was submitted for next week, so that will be a week following or starting the 12th, or after the 12th. So for the time being the Defence has no technical problems, so to speak, regarding the arrival of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then next issue, we received a motion for protective measures in which quite separate issues are dealt with. I am not going into any detail at this moment in open session. Part of the motion deals also with videolink, which, of course, is not a protective measure as such or problems like, say, of conducts of witnesses which is not a protective measure. Did I understand well, Mr. Ierace, that a response has been filed or will be filed yesterday or today so that the Chamber can consider the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that will be filed today. I note that there is an issue in respect of the first and second witnesses to be called and all the more reason why we should file it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that -- did we receive the witness list for the first week? Did we receive copies? I haven't seen any and Ms. Pilipovic usually, if the Prosecution did send you their list of witnesses with the exhibits to be used, copies would be sent -- we have received them? Yes. We have not seen them, but we have received them. It seems that those assisting us have finished -- perhaps we might pay -- we might have to pay a bit more attention to the procedure of that so that we are informed at the earliest stage about the order of appearance of witnesses. Then we have the witness, list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I know very well that we shouldn't speak about this subject in detail, except in closed session, but the Defence would like to underline a point which is important. The principle, speaking about protective measures, in fact, and I think that we have to state this clearly, for many witnesses and in fact for all of them for whom we have asked these measures, Defence is in a difficult situation. We don't have any other choice but to do this because these witnesses said, "if we are not guaranteed a protection when we come back from testifying, we will not come and testify." So this is a safe conduct issue and I am talking about the globality of the issue. I am not talking about in details. This is a general problem which applies to all of these witnesses who are in the same predicament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we are not -- we could not deal with it in a specific way, but there are some general questions. First of all, the Defence has indicated that there is a specific fear for travelling through the BiH territory because of violations of rules of the road agreements. There were no further details given in that respect. It was a very general allegation. That is one issue of which the Chamber might like to be -- to receive more specific information. And then perhaps I have to address the Prosecution and the Defence at the same time. The Chamber has never inquired in further detail about the -- about the travelling of witnesses. Is my understanding right that most of the witnesses would fly from Sarajevo to Amsterdam? Because the Chamber would like to know what territories we are talking about. I mean, if you say, "No, the usual way of travelling is we first go to Budapest and then Prague, and then we arrive in Amsterdam." Then, of course, it's a totally different issue. One of the things the Trial Chamber noticed is that there seems to be special concern about the temporary presence on the BiH territory. One of the issues that has been raised is the presence on Dutch territory. As far as the last issue is concerned, I might advise the parties to consult the host agreement which deals with the safe witnesses on Dutch territory, so no specific orders there are necessary, because that is in the host agreement between the Tribunal and the Kingdom of the Netherlands. So we would like to know exactly where the problem is as far as safe conduct. Are we just talking about travelling from Republika Srpska to Sarajevo airport or are we -- it is not clear from the submissions made until now. So it is also very difficult to give decisions in that respect. And, of course, I do not know whether the travelling schedules of the Defence witnesses will be the same as for the Prosecution witnesses. So the Chamber would like to be informed in more detail about that. Another issue that has been noticed by the Chamber is that, in most cases I would say, the protective measures sought are pseudonym and facial distortion. I would say this is the great majority. If the Prosecution files its response today, could the Chamber expect to have major objections to these type of protective measures sought? Or could we expect to have, well, let's say in 80 per cent of the case, say no objections against the facial distortion and pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is the latter. In other words we -- essentially the thrust of the submission will be not against the type of protective measures sought but the extent of the witness list to which that protective measure is sought to apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you say there are very many witnesses that are seeking protective measures. Then in general terms, the list of witnesses, we have now a list announcing 186 hours and it may have been clear to the Defence that the real bottom line would be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 170 hours. Could the Chamber first receive an explanation for this difference. Even if it is only 10 per cent, it is 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think that the Defence has tried very hard to respect what you call the "real bottom line." But the Defence cannot do more than what it can, and the Defence has tried to make it as concise as possible, and we are trying to make more efforts as we go along, as the case is developing. But as we are presenting our case. But we cannot do more before we know what your decision would be as to limiting the time. And this is quite close to what you have already announced. And the Defence still believes that the Prosecution took many more hours than the 196 hours announced, and I think that we do not think that the equality is as good as we could have expected it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is of no use to repeat what you said before, is that in your view, the Prosecution took more time. I mean, this is not a discussion where "yes or no" are really contributing to the solution of a problem. The Chamber will consider whether it will give the Defence access to their calculations. Until now, apart from your observation, that it was more than the 170 or hours, no reasons are given why you think it is more, so that is not a very useful discussion at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- If you wish me to give the exact reasons why we think that there should be more, we can give you these reasons, but it will take time. Of course, I can do it very briefly. We can think -- we can tell you what we think we will get from each witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's be short. We have two issues, first, whether the Prosecution took more time than Chamber indicated, that was what you said, that in your view, the Prosecution took more time. Now you are touching upon a different subject, and that subject is why the Defence would need more time. The Chamber will consider, we will give you an opportunity to defend that and I am not going to make any comments on this at this very moment. If you look at the statistics of the Tribunal, if you look at your list of witnesses, and especially the issues they are dealing with, you would rather expect, but we haven't heard your argument yet, that the presentation of Defence case, as in almost all cases, would take less time. But we will first consider whether we will give you an opportunity to argue on why you would need more hours, but as it stands at this moment, is that you are bound by the number of hours really as a bottom line of the time taken by the Prosecution. Then we have some complaints but the specificity of the summaries of the witnesses and the relevance of the witness statements. We have seen submissions by the Prosecution. We have seen response by the Defence, also dealing with the issue of tu quoque and reprisals and the establishment of what were military targets. Let me just try to identify what the main problems are. I think one of the first issues is that the Prosecution seem to be a bit concerned about the changes in lists, if we would compare the first provisional list of the 2nd of August, and then the other list of the 19th of September, that the Prosecution might not have been concerned that much about the witnesses that disappeared from the list, but perhaps also about the new witnesses that appeared on that list. So that is the, I would say, the consistency of the list, if the list would be changed too frequently, that would, of course, give major problems to the Prosecutor -- Prosecution to prepare for cross-examination. Then I see that the Prosecution, and that has been dealt with also in your response, is complaining about the relevance in respect of a tu quoque and your response to that. One of the other issues is that the testimony would deal with well-established matters. One of the complaints of the Prosecution is that the witnesses were only or were at least in Sarajevo prior to the time of the conflict, and, therefore, are not very relevant. The Chamber has some difficulties in predicting the relevance of the testimony. That is also because of the witness summaries provided until now. If I may just go through a few examples in order to explain what our concerns are, if I would look, for example to number 34 on your list the subject matter of the testimony is that -- perhaps I -- the witness is a resident of Pofalici. He'll testify about the attack of Muslim forces against Pofalici and about expelling of Serbs from Pofalici. This leave a lot to guess about the relevance. The Chamber is not in a position to say it is irrelevant, but at least the connection with the indictment is at least not clear. So, therefore, it is very difficult and would have similar problem, for example, with, just to draw your attention to number 47 or number 48, without going in any details. They are very short and their relevance does not become clear. That is also the reason why the Chamber has asked to provide the witness list in specific categories. Perhaps it has not become entirely clear, but the Chamber wanted to have the issues on which the witnesses were -- would testify. I would say, more or less, according to the initial list. Now we see that the last list is very much of witnesses effect, of expert witnesses. That gives no further information. The Chamber also asked to put those witnesses in order of priority. That means, the most important witness at the top, the next one down, and the less important witness at the bottom. And it will be no surprise for the Defence that the reason the Chamber asks for this to be done, is that we could, while hearing the testimony, going from the top of the list to the bottom that the Chamber could at a certain moment either establish that every new witness comes up with new important relevant material, that would be a reason to go as far as down, as that would change, if at a certain moment the evidence would become repetitious, irrelevant. Then, of course, the Chamber might consider that it has heard enough evidence on the issue at stake. On the basis of the summaries given until now, it is also very difficult for the Chamber to give a final number of hours available to the Defence. As I told you before, the bottom line would be 170 hours, but that might not be the final word in that respect. Presentation of evidence is always under the control of the Chamber and, of course, we will have to see how things develop. But perhaps at this moment, more clear information should be provided, both for the Prosecution to prepare for cross-examination, and for the Chamber to decide upon the relevance, and, therefore, whether there would be any need to reduce the number of hours. These are some general observations the Chamber would like to make. Perhaps we will have a break and then give the parties an opportunity to add whatever they want to add, what their response will be on these issues. And I might already suggest to the Defence that, of course, 92 bis could certainly help us to reduce the time needed to hear the evidence, and, of course, I do understand that you will deal with that at a later stage this week, compromising upon certain facts, of course, will reduce the need to hear evidence on these facts considerably as well. We will adjourn until 11.00, but I will first give the parties the opportunity to see whether there are any other issues on the agenda they would like to discuss after the break. Are there any subjects, apart from those we touched upon already?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will consider during the break whether we would have any additional agenda points. So we will adjourn until 11.00, and then the first thing I will do is to give the parties the opportunity to reply to the witness list, relevant time, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue the -- before we continue to discuss the list of witnesses and to give the parties an opportunity to make their submissions, I first have a question to the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic, Mr. Piletta-Zanin: The last list you provided to us, apart from the categories not specifically dealing with issues, but rather broad categories, such as witnesses of fact or expert witnesses, but on these issues is this list already in priority order, that means the most important one at the top, less important one at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence handed over the list of witnesses according to categories, which is what the Trial Chamber wanted us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But within each category?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also means that this should guide you in the calling of witnesses. I am not saying that you have to deal with one category always, but you can't call one of the lower positioned witnesses first and then the upper. So you have to -- I mean, if there are good reasons you say we go to number four before we deal with number three, that's fine. But in general terms, you should -- the calling order should be in accordance from top to bottom. Then, for both parties, the Chamber would like to receive information about two issues by next Wednesday, and that is whether any progress has been made in relation to the stipulated facts; and whether any progress has been made by -- in respect of the investigators to meet and to discuss the sources of the documents. If it would turn out by next Wednesday that no considerable progress has been made, the parties should prepare for a meeting, either with the SLO or with one of the Judges on Thursday morning to see what progress can be made. So, please, take care of that in filling your agendas. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you will have an opportunity before I give a final opportunity to the parties to make any further submissions on the list of witnesses. You will first have an opportunity for, well, let's say, ten minutes to explain why you might need or you will need more time than the Prosecution took for the presentation of their case. So perhaps we first hear that so that the Prosecution would also be in a position to respond to that part, if making further submissions at a later stage this morning. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to do it now, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be very brief. The reason why we believe that this number of hours is necessary to us is based on two elements. The first one was the assessment or the estimate that we made, as accurately as we were able to, of what our witnesses will be able to say. And the second of these elements is, of course, has to be factored in the surprise effect because we know very well that what can happen during cross-examination, a witness of one side can say a lot more than what was expected, a lot less, or completely -- something completely different. So this is a kind of strategic reserve that we need. It is a kind of oxygen tank, so that we can make a balance with other witnesses, also on important issues as important as shelling. As I told you already, it is probable that during the case of the Prosecution -- case of the Defence can be diminished as we -- so there shouldn't be any surprises during cross-examinations, but this was one of the points. Another point which seems even more important now is the need -- and here, Mr. President, I still don't have your decision in my hands. I am just deducing. This is just by deduction that I am making, this is an assumption that I am making these observations. Now, with regard to shelling incidents, for one reason or another, you may have decided that there was a campaign or at least that there are reasons to believe that there was a campaign, which would then implicate that there was a will, an intention to inflict terror on the population. Therefore, our witnesses who are mostly soldiers, military personnel who were on the front lines, it will be necessary for them to come and speak here before your Chamber. Then each of the companies here did not have an order to fire at such-and-such a target, allegedly civilian, but this is essential, that each one of these soldiers will come and that they did know the number of legitimate targets in the city, which will then give the appearance that there was a random shelling or that it could have represented what we call a campaign or that it was just an importance, that it can be interpreted by a Chamber that it was -- there was intention to inflict terror on civilian population. Now these witnesses should then even be worked on more by the Defence that is in relation to your decision, if I am assessing it correctly. So if we ask them here, was there a military target, yes, and so on and so on. So this is a little bit we still have some blind spots because we don't know very well how this exercise is going to be carried out. And perhaps we will have more insight as of next week. But this is just the general outlines. Another matter that you mentioned, we will try and save time. The 34, the Pofalici, now this considering that there was a very rough presentation of facts, the Pofalici is going to be very important because the witness is going to be able to say, what are the shellings that they suffered, and this is not tu quoque, it is a different thing. He will be able to say that equally, how many shellings occurred by error in the area they were defending. These were technical errors that happened on one side, so they happened on the other as well. It may happen that this witness will come and say yes, these shellings did take place by mistake on civilian areas and this is a mistake. So this is very important for us to say that such-and-such a shelling that happened, happened -- also happened by error. Am I to stop or should I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could just slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I had the Serbian language -- I was listening to the Serbian language. So that's it. I understood your gesture, Mr. President. I interpreted that as an invitation for me to stop, but it wasn't, but certainly I am going to stop here, because I think that we said enough, and I hope that we were clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. A bit surprising that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. after the summer you stop even without being invited to, but then I remember I wished you a relaxed summer at the 2nd of August. Then I would like to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to make any further submissions in respect of the list of witnesses, and then finally given an opportunity to Defence to respond to that or to make whatever further submissions they would like to make in this respect. And if there would be nothing else on the agenda, we would then conclude this pre-defence conference. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I assume that you also expect to hear from me within those ten minutes on the sufficiency of the Rule 65 ter descriptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is part of the -- part of the submissions you made in writing before and I would like to give you -- although, I did limit Mr. Piletta-Zanin to ten minutes, which he didn't even use, for the specific reasons why the Defence made the reservations as far as the time allocated to them was concerned. I would give a bit more time to both parties to make further submissions, so if that would be a quarter of an hour, 20 minutes, it would be no problem. So don't feel that much limited making these further submissions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fact, I think I will be very brief. The explanation just given by the Defence in relation to the anticipated evidence of Witness 34 firstly, illustrates the insufficiency of the summary of facts which appears alongside that person's name. Secondly, raises further issues as to the nature of that evidence in terms of its internal logic. Firstly, in respect of the description which was filed, that is the summary of facts which was filed, on the basis of that summary of facts, it is impossible, in my respectful submission, to elicit from it anything of relevance to the case. Using that as an example, the Prosecution is of the view that it may well be that its cross-examination of witnesses called by the Defence will be limited. The Prosecution does not intend to cross-examine for the sake of using up the time it is allocated. Yesterday, I indicated to the Defence that it should be ready to call its witnesses in quick succession for that reason. By the same token when witnesses who, at least the Prosecution regards as being of more substance and relevance, the Prosecution would respectfully seek leave on some occasions to go beyond the allocated time, that is, beyond the period of time which the Defence takes in chief, with the overall objective of keeping well within the same period of time that the Defence takes with its witnesses, examining them in chief. So, Mr. President, on the face of it it is difficult to conclude otherwise, that is, on the face of the schedule of facts filed, it is difficult to not conclude that the only possible significance of the witness's evidence is one indeed of one of tu quoque. Mr. Piletta-Zanin enlightens us with a further development of the written schedule of facts to tell us that the witness will say that he was on the front line, as I understand it, and that he observed Muslim forces, using the term used by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, accidentally hit civilians when they intended to hit legitimate targets. One wonders how a witness, in the position described by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could come to such conclusions. He goes on to anticipate the witness's evidence to be in effect that, therefore, the same applied to gunners within the SRK, that quite clearly, apparently, where they hit civilian targets, it was because of some inbuilt factor of inaccuracy. This raises a new issue as to relevance which, no doubt, we will face at the appropriate time when such evidence is sought to be elicited, namely, on what basis, more specifically, on what proper basis, could a witness give such evidence, but perhaps that should wait until a later time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. May I just ask you one question: We discussed a few examples of very brief witness summaries. Would you have any specific problem with one of the witnesses that is on the list for the first week?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that is covered in the motion filed in which I analyzed, to some extent, the summaries of fact, and came to the view to illustrate the point that there were only five witnesses who, on the strength of the summaries of fact, challenged the Prosecution case. The summaries of fact identify issues, and no more. Some of those issues seem to lack any relevance. Other issues clearly could have relevance, but because the summaries don't specify the facts or summarise the facts on which the witness will give evidence, it is impossible to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I might interrupt you. Of course, the Chamber has read this and of course we have also compared it a bit with the Prosecution witnesses summaries, and it appears that sometimes they are very much focussing on facts. For example, if you are talking about sniping incidents or shelling incidents we find that a lot of what we can expect from them as factual information is clearly indicated. Of course, the Chamber also noticed that there are not many witnesses, as far as we can see that will testify about the specific circumstances of specific shelling or sniping incidents, although it is indicated that sometimes the testimony might have some relevance in respect of these incidents as well. On the other hand, we also see that as far as the Prosecution witnesses are concerned, sometimes we also find issues, rather than facts. For example, utility supply, you will tell us about utility supply without giving us any further details and what facts we should expect, but just about the general issue of shelling. I think that we should keep in mind that sometimes the subject matter of the testimony might make it more difficult to give specific facts. On the other hand, and I am now looking in the direction of the Defence, sometimes the issues are very broad and very general where further details. For example, if I am just -- if you are talking about utilities and you add to it that it is water and electricity, then already gas is off and water and electricity are specifically mentioned, so even on the issues you can be more specific. I think we have to keep both in mind when working on the summaries because I think some work still has to be done, since it would be too difficult for the Prosecution to prepare for cross-examination. On the other hand, the Prosecution should bear in mind that some issues make the more difficult to come up with specific facts than others, as we noticed that similar approach could be found in the Prosecution witness list summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the latter point first, while it is so that some of the Prosecution 65 ter summaries were broad in that sense, equally, I think it could fairly be said that many of them, if not most of them, were quite detailed. In relation to the witnesses who are to be called next week, perhaps it would be useful to focus on the first two or three. In respect of the first witness, there is a lengthy summary of facts, one long paragraph, which gives some background to the witness, which, in itself, doesn't appear to be particularly relevant. And then we have statements such as this: "He is familiar with the role of JNA," moving on "he was an eyewitness of mutual shelling and sniping," which really doesn't assist anyone as to what it is the witness will say. Will he talk about the issues which are in the indictment? Namely who was responsible for the shelling and sniping of civilians, or indeed more basically, whether that happened or not, we don't know. In the same sentence, "he was an eyewitness to forced mobilisation, taking people on forced labor," what is the relevance of that? The Prosecution states that that is not relevant to the issues in the indictment. And then finally we have this all encompassing sentence: "The witness also knows the other relevant events which happened during the conflict when he was in Sarajevo." That is of no assistance to the Prosecution in preparing its cross-examination. The second witness to be called that is Witness number 5, I think yes, number 5. Again, we don't know what it is in effect that she really will say. We are told that she will take about ABiH actions from their positions against the Grbavica area, about ABiH sniping. What does that mean, if I could pause there? Does that mean sniping against Serb civilians, it is sniping against Serb forces, that is armed combatants or what? The third witness - excuse me - is Witness number 2. We are told that he was at the Kosevo clinic in Sarajevo. "The witness is familiar with the circumstances in Sarajevo as well as the circumstances in Kosevo clinic, immediately before the conflicts broke out and during the war too." Again, that is of no assistance. Is he to talk about mobile mortars which are alleged? Is he to talk about ABiH forces allegedly targeting the hospital? We don't know. Reading on: "He was an eyewitness of shelling and sniping on the warring side." On the face of it that's of absolutely no relevance. It is not clear whether it's lawful of shelling or sniping, in other words, of combatants or not. So, Mr. President, perhaps if the Defence might be requested to provide proper summaries of fact in relation to the first three witnesses, that would serve two purposes, firstly, giving proper notice to the Prosecution, and secondly, it might assist as process in developing an appropriate understanding with the Defence as to what is required. Mr. President, could I just go back to one earlier issue, briefly, and that is, that whatever shortcomings there were in the 65 ter summaries of the Prosecution has to be seen in the context that the Prosecution were provided with statements and also supplemental information sheets. And they, of course, were not provided to the Trial Chamber, as is required, but there is no dispute that witness statements, in some cases, many witness statements, as well as a supplemental information sheet were provided. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you mean that the Defence was provided with the statements and the supplemental information sheet. Ms. Pilipovic, I would like to hear the response from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, response in relation to supplemental information of what Mr. Ierace spoke about more generally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to make on the issue of the witness list and the complaints about it and related issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, I have to tell you that we are rather surprised and this is just in the first three cases, even if we just talk about the first case. If we look at this witness, we can see that there are elements here that are very far from being irrelevant. We know what he was, we know what his duties were, what he did, and to use the expression that the Prosecution used, when we are talking about "mutual shelling," it is precisely here with the problem lies. We are being told that this is irrelevant, and I believe, and again I am walking on uncharted ground, and I have to do this because it is still depending on what says in your decision, but this is where the crux of the problem lies. If there were mutual shellings, were there also errors? Were there risks of errors? Perhaps this witness could say that there was shelling coming from the other side, that there was an error, that this was mistaken, and I believe that this is a very useful element, if not necessary, for the Defence to state our position, which is just to remind you is that there were possible firing near civilian targets and that there were errors, not voluntary, not intentional. Now, if we have a list of every shelling from such-and-such a date, such-and-such an hour, this is really impossible. This is not the same as the position of the Prosecution, which decided to have five shelling incidents, and then more for the other incidents, sniping incidents. So, really, the position of the Defence is different. The principles are different. We had the Defence of principle, basing ourselves on very specific incidents, cases, but it is absolutely impossible that we can say every time on such-and-such a date, there was a shelling and so on. The witnesses couldn't possibly remember, and to ask such a degree of accuracy, I don't think that is conceivable. So I think here, for this very first case we have been sufficiently detailed, sufficiently precise, and the Prosecution knows what this is about. So that the principle of the Defence has clearly been established. And if it has not been understood, I can explain it again. It may happen that there are other witnesses whom there is more information necessary. Now, less information. Now, for instance, we can say for this specific witness we wouldn't like to know precisely such-and-such things, and this is the witness in such a case where perhaps that would be more useful for everyone and more constructive. So this is what I wanted to say, in principle and generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, the parties, if the Defence is about to establish that errors were made in targeting of shells, is that in dispute between the parties? I mean does the Prosecution, in general terms, because we are talking in general terms now and not on a specific incident, contest that such errors are made?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is not contested by the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fear that this will not take us forward. What we would like to know is what it says in the decision, what you have said in the decision about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you will not find anything in your decision about errors on targeting, any determination in that respect of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. But I think that perhaps the Chamber spoke about the quantity of the firing and perhaps about the outgoing and the incoming fire and the proportion thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps this is not the very moment to discuss these kind of matters. I would like as a matter of fact, to sit the parties together in respect of the first witnesses, because we have to develop a practice which is -- which enables the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness effectively and not to be with empty hands and be taken by surprise. So perhaps I would like to invite the parties to do this very early at this very moment, even without having a written statement, that perhaps questions like you have raised today, for example -- I would agree with you that a part of the statement which says he was an eyewitness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. between shelling and sniping between the warring sides, that of course, could cover the whole armed conflict, without any further specification, it might be very difficult for the Prosecution to respond -- to prepare for cross-examination of such a witness. So, therefore -- and the Chamber is also aware that the Defence, of course had the witness statements given before and could confront the witness with the earlier statements. So, therefore, I would like the parties to see whether questions such as raised by the Prosecution today could be resolved. If that is not possible, then I will take care that, tomorrow, the Senior Legal Officer or one of the Judges will be there in order to guide the parties as how to proceed in this respect. We can't deal with that until next Thursday because the first witnesses will be examined on from the 7th of October. But the Chamber wants to prevent that we have to lose time later on because the information was not sufficient to prepare for cross-examination. So specifically for the first week, I would like the parties to sit together and to see whether, even if it would be early, additional information could be given so the Prosecution is better able to prepare, if this would result in clashes rather than in fruitful cooperation, than the Chamber is available to assist the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so I clearly understand that, you anticipate that the parties should meet today, and if we can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or tomorrow. Or tomorrow. And I expect the parties that if they don't solve the problems, that they -- if the Chamber or a Senior Legal Officer is able, then the parties should make themselves available as well, even if it would be at extraordinary times. The Chamber is determined to solve these kinds of problems, rather than to spend more time on discussing them. Yes. Is there any other issue the parties would like to raise at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. There is one matter, or even perhaps two. The first matter or the first question that we should address is the assistance that the Defence would like to have from your Chamber, in a sense that the Defence wanted to call as witnesses a number of people from the UN family. These people knew the situation. They were high-ranking military personnel and the Defence has not been able to find the addresses of these persons, who were not able to contact them directly and what will certainly come up is the assistance of your Chamber that the Defence will need.
